issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, the trigger pattern is not clinically well matched: 'Military Topics' suggests combat/war-related trauma cues, and 'Loss Themes' suggests bereavement-related reminders, while no trigger references fumes, smells, contamination, breathing difficulty, workplaces, or chemical hazards. This makes the trigger set hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat items are internally coherent with a persecution/assault-style danger formulation ('someone is following me', needing to stay alert at night) rather than a toxic exposure formulation. They do not plausibly connect to the selected triggers, despite the strong Triggers → Threat edge that should link these nodes tightly.

issues.item: Triggers: Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
issues.explanation: The trigger item about discussions of people losing loved ones is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of toxic chemical exposure. It implies bereavement-related trauma content that is not otherwise represented in the profile, making this trigger clinically implausible for the same patient unless the exposure involved deaths, which is not supported elsewhere.

Within the Threat node, concentration difficulty is a broad nonspecific symptom, whereas sleep vigilance reflects an ongoing sense of current external danger. That combination can coexist, but in this profile the threat content is otherwise sparse and the selected triggers do not clearly support a coherent toxic-exposure-related danger schema, weakening internal coherence.

vignette:
Layla is a 51-year-old hotel manager who had been with the same downtown property for nearly two decades when the incident occurred. It happened on a humid Tuesday in late summer, during a routine inspection of the housekeeping storage room. A maintenance worker had improperly mixed two cleaning agents-an industrial bleach and an ammonia-based disinfectant-and the chemical reaction released a cloud of chloramine gas into the confined space. Layla walked in just as the mixture began to fume. She inhaled deeply before she could turn and run. Her throat immediately seized; her eyes streamed; she could not stop coughing long enough to call for help. A colleague found her on the floor, gasping, and called 911. She spent the next three days in the hospital, on oxygen, breathing the sharp, sterile air of the ICU while her lungs slowly recovered. The antiseptic smell of the hospital became, in her mind, the smell of being unable to breathe.

In the weeks afterward, Layla returned to work because she felt she had no choice. The hotel could not afford to lose its manager, and she told herself that getting back in the building was the only way to prove she was still capable. But the storage room door had been repainted and the chemicals were now locked away in a ventilated cabinet. Every time she walked past that corridor, her chest tightened. She began delegating all housekeeping inspections to her assistant, inventing reasons why she was too busy with paperwork. The trigger, she noticed, was not only the storage room. It was the workday itself: the stress of a late-arriving shipment or a guest complaint would suddenly feel unbearable, as if her body were bracing for another chemical cloud. And any unexpected loud sound-the slam of a service door, the clatter of a dropped tray in the kitchen-made her heart pound so hard she had to sit down. She started spending more time in her office with the door shut, monitoring the hallway through the small window rather than walking out into it.

At home, the vigilance did not stop. Her husband, Karim, had always been a sound sleeper, but Layla could not let herself drift off before he was asleep, and even then she lay awake listening. She began sleeping on the side of the bed closest to the door, facing the entrance, telling herself it was just a habit. The real reason, she admitted only to herself, was that she needed to be ready-ready for what, she could not say, but her body insisted. If Karim moved suddenly in his sleep or if a car backfired outside, she would be on her feet in seconds, palms sweating, certain that something toxic or violent was about to flood the room. She stopped letting him cook with strong spices because the pungent aromas reminded her of the chemical smell in the storage room, though she never said that aloud.

The consequence that finally brought her to seek help was her job itself. A district manager visited for a quarterly review and commented that Layla seemed distracted, that she had stopped walking the property. One of the housekeepers had mentioned that the manager never came near the cleaning stations anymore. Layla invented a plausible story about seasonal allergies, but she knew it would not hold. She began calling in sick on days she had to attend safety meetings, terrified that being in the training room-where cleaning products were discussed-would trigger another attack of dizziness and coughing. Her marriage, too, felt thin. Karim had started sleeping in the guest room because she kept waking him with her restlessness. He did not understand why she flinched when he touched her shoulder from behind.

What Layla fears most as she sits in the therapist's office is not the memory itself but the belief that her body has permanently changed-that she will never walk through her own hotel without scanning for hazards, never fall asleep without her ears straining for a sound, never be the manager she was before. She hopes, uncertainly, that someone can help her stop feeling like the chemical cloud is still in the room with her.
